subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The 'welfare state' refers to:
options: A system where the government provides services and benefits to support citizens' wellbeing
questions.explain: The welfare state is a system in which the state provides services such as healthcare, education and benefits to support its citizens.

questions.q: The Marxist view of stratification argues that the main divide in capitalist society is between:
questions.explain: Marx argued society is divided by ownership of the means of production into the bourgeoisie and the proletariat.

questions.q: The 'cycle of deprivation' suggests that poverty:
options: Can be passed from one generation to the next in a repeating cycle
questions.explain: The cycle of deprivation describes how disadvantages can be transmitted from parents to children, trapping families in poverty.

questions.q: 'Absolute poverty' is best defined as:
options: Being poorer than most people in your society
Lacking the minimum needed to survive, such as food, shelter and clothing
questions.explain: Absolute poverty means lacking the basic essentials needed for survival.

questions.q: The 'dependency culture' argument claims that generous welfare may:
options: Discourage some people from seeking work by making them reliant on benefits
Always lift everyone out of poverty
questions.explain: The dependency culture thesis, linked to the New Right, argues over-generous benefits can discourage self-reliance and work.

questions.q: A Marxist criticism of the welfare state is that it:
options: Helps maintain capitalism by keeping the workforce healthy and reducing unrest
Only benefits the working class fully
questions.explain: Marxists argue welfare can prop up capitalism by keeping workers fit for exploitation and dampening discontent.

questions.q: A 'meritocracy' is a society in which positions are supposedly allocated according to:
questions.explain: In a meritocracy, rewards and positions are based on talent and effort rather than birth.

questions.q: In sociology, the difference between 'wealth' and 'income' is that:
options: Wealth is the total value of assets owned; income is money received regularly (e.g. wages)
Income is always larger than wealth
questions.explain: Wealth is the stock of assets a person owns, while income is the flow of money received, such as wages or benefits.

questions.q: In Weber's terms, 'authority' differs from coercion because authority is:
options: Power that is seen as legitimate and accepted by people
questions.explain: Weber defined authority as legitimate power that people accept as rightful, unlike coercion based on force.

questions.q: 'Ascribed status' means status that is:
options: Fixed at birth or given regardless of effort (e.g. inherited title)
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed at birth or assigned independent of a person's efforts, unlike achieved status.

questions.q: 'Relative poverty' means being poor:
options: Only when unable to survive at all
Compared with the general standard of living in one's society
questions.explain: Relative poverty is measured against the typical standard of living in a particular society.

questions.q: 'Intergenerational social mobility' specifically measures movement:
options: Within a single person's own working life
Between the class of children and that of their parents
questions.explain: Intergenerational mobility compares a person's class position with that of their parents across generations.

questions.q: In Weber's view of stratification, social class is based on:
options: A person's market situation, especially their skills and qualifications
Ownership of the means of production alone
questions.explain: Weber argued class position depends on a person's market situation, including their skills and qualifications, not just ownership.

questions.q: 'Life chances' refers to:
options: The number of years someone lives
Random opportunities given by the government
A person's likelihood of obtaining things society values, like health, education and wealth
A person's luck in games of chance
questions.explain: Life chances are the opportunities (or lack of them) people have to obtain valued things like good health, education and income.

questions.q: Weber identified three types of legitimate authority. Which is the correct set?
questions.explain: Weber distinguished legal-rational, traditional and charismatic authority as the three sources of legitimate power.

questions.q: Weber argued that stratification has three dimensions. Which set is correct?
questions.explain: Weber identified class, status and party (power) as three separate dimensions of social stratification.

questions.q: 'Status' in sociology usually refers to:
options: The social position or honour attached to a person or role
The amount of money someone has only
questions.explain: Status refers to the social position and prestige attached to a person or role, which can differ from wealth.

questions.q: A criticism of Davis and Moore's functionalist theory of stratification is that it:
options: Ignores the role of ability entirely
Overlooks how inherited wealth and unequal chances mean rewards are not based purely on merit
questions.explain: Critics argue Davis and Moore ignore how inheritance and unequal opportunities prevent rewards reflecting genuine merit.

questions.q: 'Universal benefits' are welfare payments that are:
options: Available to everyone in a category regardless of income (e.g. some forms of child benefit)
Only ever given to the very rich
questions.explain: Universal benefits are given to all people in a particular group regardless of their income, unlike means-tested benefits.

questions.q: The 'culture of poverty' explanation argues that poverty is partly caused by:
options: A complete lack of any wealthy people
A set of values and attitudes (e.g. fatalism) passed on among the poor
questions.explain: The culture of poverty thesis (Oscar Lewis) suggests some poor groups develop values, like fatalism, that help reproduce poverty.

questions.q: The functionalist theory of stratification by Davis and Moore argues that inequality is:
options: Necessary and functional because it motivates the most able to fill important roles
A myth that does not exist
Caused only by the ruling class
questions.explain: Davis and Moore argued unequal rewards are functional, ensuring the most able people are motivated to take society's important roles.

questions.q: Which statement about the gender pay gap is most accurate?
options: The gap was abolished in the 1900s
Men and women have always earned exactly the same
Women on average still tend to earn less than men over their careers
questions.explain: On average women still tend to earn less than men, reflecting ongoing gender inequality in pay.
